# [Monday 23 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/23/)

Up before day, and by coach to [Sir W. Coventry’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/), and with him to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there walked a great while with him in the garden till the [Commissioners of the Treasury](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11226/) met, and there talked over many businesses, and particularly he tells me that by my desire he hath moved the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) that [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) might be removed from the Navy, at least the [Controller’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/485/) place, and his business put on my [Lord Brouncker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) and [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/); that the [Committee for Accounts](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/12029/) are good sober men, and such as he thinks we shall have fair play from; that he hopes that the kingdom will escape ruin in general, notwithstanding all our fears, and yet I find he do seem not very confident in it. So to the Commissioners of the Treasury, and there I had a dispute before them with [Sir Stephen Fox](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/848/) about our orders for money, who is very angry, but I value it not. But, Lord! to see with what folly my [Lord Albemarle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/) do speak in this business would make a man wonder at the good fortune of such a fool. Thence meeting there with [Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/), he and I to [the Exchange](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1085/), and there I saw [Carr](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11437/) stand in the pillory for the business of my [Lord Gerard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5794/), which is supposed will make a hot business in the [House of Commons](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/292/), when they shall come to sit again, the [Lords](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/293/) having ordered this with great injustice, as all people think, his only fault being the printing his petition before, by accident, his petition be read in the House. Here walked up and down the Exchange with Creed, and then [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and there hear by Creed that the Bishops [of Winchester](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5744/) and [of Rochester, and the Dean of the Chapel](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10263/), and some other great prelates, are suspended: and a cloud upon [the Archbishop](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2519/) ever since the late business in the House of Lords; and I believe it will be a heavy blow to the Clergy. This noon I bought [a sermon](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11955/) of [Dr. Floyd’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10568/), which Creed read a great part of to me and [Mr. Hollier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1536/), who dined with me, but as well writ and as good, against the Church of Rome, as ever I read; but, Lord! how Hollier, poor man, was taken with it. They gone I to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and there very late with [Mr. Willson](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6487/) and my people about the making of a new contract for the [victualler](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9082/), which do and will require a great deal of pains of me, and so to supper and to bed, [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) being pretty well all this day by reason of her imposthume being broke in her cheek into her mouth. This day, at the ’Change, Creed shewed me [Mr. Coleman](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11315/), of whom my wife hath so good an opinion, and says that he is as very a rogue for women as any in the world; which did disquiet me, like a fool, and run in my mind a great while.

# [Tuesday 24 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/24/)

Up, and all the morning at [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and at noon with my clerks to dinner, and then to the office again, busy at the office till six at night, and then by coach to [St. James’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/466/), it being about six at night; my design being to see the ceremonys, this night being the eve of [Christmas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/), at the [Queen’s chapel](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7305/). But it being not begun I to [Westminster Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/), and there staid and walked, and then to [the Swan](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1707/), and there drank and talked, and did banter [L&M say “besar”. P.G.] a little [Frank](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10614/), and so to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and sent my coach round, I through [the Park](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/248/) to chapel, where I got in up almost to the rail, and with a great deal of patience staid from nine at night to two in the morning, in a very great crowd; and there expected, but found nothing extraordinary, there being nothing but a high masse. [The Queen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2381/) was there, and some ladies. But, Lord! what an odde thing it was for me to be in a crowd of people, here a footman, there a beggar, here a fine lady, there a zealous poor [papist](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/306/), and here a [Protestant](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7980/), two or three together, come to see the shew. I was afeard of my pocket being picked very much … [But here I did make myself to do la cosa by mere imagination, miranda a jolie mosa and with my yes open, which I never did before — and God forgive me for it, it being in the chapel. – L&M] Their musique very good indeed, but their service I confess too frivolous, that there can be no zeal go along with it, and I do find by them themselves that they do run over their beads with one hand, and point and play and talk and make signs with the other in the midst of their masse. But all things very rich and beautiful; and I see the papists have the wit, most of them, to bring cushions to kneel on, which I wanted, and was mightily troubled to kneel. All being done, and I sorry for my coming, missing of what I expected; which was, to have had a child born and dressed there, and a great deal of do: but we broke up, and nothing like it done: and there I left people receiving the Sacrament: and the Queen gone, and ladies; only my [Lady Castlemayne](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1062/), who looked prettily in her night-clothes, and so took my coach, which waited, and away through [Covent Garden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/126/), to set down two gentlemen and a lady, who come thither to see also, and did make mighty mirth in their talk of the folly of this religion. And so I stopped, having set them down and drank some burnt [wine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/) at the [Rose Tavern](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11956/) door, while the [constables](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/14184/) come, and two or three Bellmen went by… [Continued [tomorrow](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/25/). P.G.]

# [Wednesday 25 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/25/)

[Continued from [yesterday](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/24/). P.G.] …it being a fine, light, moonshine morning, and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) round [the city](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/275/), and stopped and dropped money at five or six places, which I was the willinger to do, it being [Christmas-day](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/), and so home, and there find [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) in bed, and [Jane](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/149/) and the maids making pyes, and so I to bed, and slept well, and rose about nine, and to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/), and there heard a dull sermon of [Mr. Mills](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1215/), but a great many fine people at church; and so home. # [Thursday 26 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/26/)

Up and to Westminster, and there to [the Swan](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1050/), and by chance met [Mr. Spicer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1078/) and another [’Chequer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/290/) clerk, and there made them drink, and there talked of the credit the ’Chequer is now come to and will in a little time, and so away homeward, and called at [my bookseller’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11465/), and there bought [Mr. Harrington’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7047/) works, [“Oceana,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11562/)&c., and two other books, which cost me 4 _l._, and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and there eat a bit, and then with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) to the [King’s playhouse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/475/), and there saw [“The Surprizall;”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11025/) which did not please me to-day, the actors not pleasing me; and especially [Nell’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5037/) acting of a serious part, which she spoils. Here met with [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/), and sat by him, and home by coach with him, and there to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) a while, and then home to supper and to bed. I hear this day that [Mrs. Stewart](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5036/) do at this day keep a great court at [Somerset House](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/243/), with her husband the [Duke of Richmond](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6590/), she being visited for her beauty’s sake by people, as [the Queen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2381/) is, at nights; and they say also that she is likely to go to Court again, and there put my [Lady Castlemayne’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1062/) nose out of joynt. God knows that would make a great turn. This day I was invited to have gone to my cozen [Mary Pepys’](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2934/) burial, my uncle [Thomas’](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2542/) daughter, but could not.

# [Friday 27 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/27/)

Up, and by water to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there walked with [Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/) in the [Matted gallery](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5840/) till by and by a [Committee for Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5243/) met: the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) there; and there I did discourse over to them their condition as to money, which they were all mightily, as I could desire, satisfied with, but the [Duke of Albemarle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/), who takes the part of the Guards against us in our supplies of money, which is an odd consideration for a dull, heavy blockhead as he is, understanding no more of either than a goose: but the ability and integrity of [Sir W. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/), in all [the King’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) concernments, I do and must admire. After the Committee up, I and Sir W. Coventry walked an hour in the gallery, talking over many businesses, and he tells me that there are so many things concur to make him and his Fellow Commissioners unable to go through the King’s work that he do despair of it, every body becoming an enemy to them in their retrenchments, and the King unstable, the debts great and the King’s present occasions for money great and many and pressing, the bankers broke and every body keeping in their money, while the times are doubtful what will stand. But he says had they come in two years ago they doubt not to have done what the King would by this time, or were the King in the condition as heretofore, when [the Chancellor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/804/) was great, to be able to have what sums of money they pleased of the [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/), and then the ill administration was such that instead of making good use of this power and money he suffered all to go to ruin. But one such sum now would put all upon their legs, and now the King would have the Parliament give him money when they are in an ill humour and will not be willing to give any, nor are very able, and besides every body distrusts what they give the King will be lost; whereas six months hence, when they see that the King can live without them, and is become steady, and to manage what he has well, he doubts not but their doubts would be removed, and would be much more free as well as more able to give him money. He told me how some of his enemies at the Duke of York’s had got the Duke of York’s commission for the Commissioners of his estate changed, and he and [Brouncker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) and [Povy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5263/) left out: that this they did do to disgrace and impose upon him at this time; but that he, though he values not the thing, did go and tell the Duke of York what he heard, and that he did not think that he had given him any reason to do this, out of his belief that he would not be as faithful and serviceable to him as the best of those that have got him put out. Whereupon the Duke of York did say that it arose only from his not knowing whether now he would have time to regard his affairs; and that, if he should, he would put him into the commission with his own hand, though the commission be passed. He answered that he had been faithful to him, and done him good service therein, so long as he could attend it; and if he had been able to have attended it more, he would not have enriched himself with such and such estates as my Lord Chancellor hath got, that did properly belong to his Royal Highness, as being forfeited to the King, and so by the King’s gift given to the Duke of York. Hereupon the Duke of York did call for the commission, and hath since put him in. This he tells me he did only to show his enemies that he is not so low as to be trod on by them, or the Duke hath any so bad opinion of him as they would think.

Here we parted, and I with [Sir H. Cholmly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5179/) went and took a turn into [the Park](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/248/), and there talked of several things, and about [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) particularly, and of his management of his business, and among other discourse about the method he will leave his accounts in if he should suddenly die, he says there is nothing but what is easily understood, but only a sum of 500 _l._ which he has entered given to E. E. S., which in great confidence he do discover to me to be my [Lord Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), at the beginning of their contract for the [Mole](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5384/), and I suppose the rest did the like, which was 1500 _l._, which would appear a very odd thing for my Lord to be a profiter by the getting of the contract made for them. But here it puts me into thoughts how I shall own my receiving of 200 _l._ a year from him, but it is his gift, I never asked of him, and which he did to Mr. Povy, and so there is no great matter in it. Thence to other talk. He tells me that the business of getting the [Duchess of Richmond](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5036/) to Court is broke off, [the Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6590/) not suffering it; and thereby great trouble is brought among the people that endeavoured it, and thought they had compassed it. And, Lord! to think that at this time the King should mind no other cares but these! He tells me that my [Lord of Canterbury](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2519/) is a mighty stout man, and a man of a brave, high spirit, and cares not for this disfavour that he is under at Court, knowing that the King cannot take away his profits during his life, and therefore do not value it.[1](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/#fn1-1667-12-27)

Thence I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and there to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) and wrote a letter to the Duke of York from myself about my clerks extraordinary, which I have employed this war, to prevent my being obliged to answer for what others do without any reason demand allowance for, and so by this means I will be accountable for none but my own, and they shall not have them but upon the same terms that I have, which is a profession that with these helps they will answer to their having performed their duties of their places. So to dinner, and then away by coach to the [Temple](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/131/), and then for speed by water thence to White Hall, and there to our usual attending the Duke of York, and did attend him, where among other things I did present and lodge my letter, and did speed in it as I could wish. Thence home with [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) and [Comm. Middleton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7120/) by coach, and there home and to [cards](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/797/) with my [wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), [W. Hewer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1082/), [Mercer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7761/), and [the girle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11640/), and mighty pleasant all the evening, and so to bed with my wife, which I have not done since her being ill for three weeks or thereabouts.

1.   This character of Archbishop Sheldon does not tally with the scandal that Pepys previously reported of him. Burnet has some passages of importance on this in his “Own Time,” Book II. He affirms that Charles’s final decision to throw over Clarendon was caused by the Chancellor’s favouring Mrs. Stewart’s marriage with the Duke of Richmond. The king had a conference with Sheldon on the removal of Clarendon, but could not convert the archbishop to his view. Lauderdale told Burnet that he had an account of the interview from the king. “The king and Sheldon had gone into such expostulations upon it that from that day forward Sheldon could never recover the king’s confidence.” [↩](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/#fnr1-1667-12-27)

# [Saturday 28 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/28/)

Up, and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where busy all the morning, at noon [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and there to dinner with my clerks and [Mr. Pelling](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11258/), and had a very good dinner, among others a haunch of [venison](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/383/) boiled, and merry we were, and I rose soon from dinner, and with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and [girle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11640/) to the [King’s house](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/475/), and there saw [“The Mad Couple,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11618/) which is but an ordinary play; but only [Nell’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5037/) and [Hart’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11087/) mad parts are most excellently done, but especially hers: which makes it a miracle to me to think how ill she do any serious part, as, the other day, just like a fool or changeling; and, in a mad part, do beyond all imitation almost. [It pleased us mightily to see the natural affection of a poor woman, the mother of one of the children brought on the stage: the child crying, she by force got upon the stage, and took up her child and carried it away off of the stage from Hart.]

Many fine faces here to-day. Thence home, and there to the office late, and then home to supper and to bed.

I am told to-day, which troubles me, that great complaint is made upon [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), among our merchants, that the very [Ostend](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7827/) little pickaroon men-of-war do offer violence to our merchant-men, and search them, beat our masters, and plunder them, upon pretence of carrying Frenchmen’s goods. Lord! what a condition are we come to, and that so soon after a war!

# [Sunday 29 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/29/)

(Lord’s day). Up, and at my chamber all the day, both morning and afternoon (only a little at dinner with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) alone), upon the settling of my [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) accounts towards the evening of all reckonings now against the new year, and here I do see the great folly of letting things go long unevened, it being very hard for me and dangerous to state after things are gone out of memory, and much more would be so should I have died in this time and my accounts come to other hands, to understand which would never be. At night comes [Mrs. Turner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3028/) to see us; and there, among other talk, she tells me that [Mr. William Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2514/), who is lately come over from Ireland, is a [Quaker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/305/) again, or some very melancholy thing; that he cares for no company, nor comes into any which is a pleasant thing, after his being abroad so long, and [his father](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) such a hypocritical rogue, and at this time an [Atheist](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/368/). She gone, I to my very great content do find my accounts to come very even and naturally, and so to supper and to bed.

# [Monday 30 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/30/)

Up before day, and by coach to Westminster, and there first to [Sir H. Cholmly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5179/), and there I did to my great content deliver him up his little several papers for sums of money paid him, and took his regular receipts upon his orders, wherein I am safe. Thence to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there to visit [Sir G. Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/), and there was with him a great while, and [my Lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4039/) and they seem in very good humour, but by and by Sir G. Carteret and I alone, and there we did talk of the ruinous condition we are in, [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) being going to put out of the Council so many able men; such as my [Lord Anglesey](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/887/), [Ashly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/215/), [Hollis](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/886/), [Secretary Morrice](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5947/) (to bring in [Mr. Trevor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11972/)), and the [Archbishop of Canterbury](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2519/), and my [Lord Bridgewater](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11086/). He tells me that this is true, only the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) do endeavour to hinder it, and the Duke of York himself did tell him so: that the King and the Duke of York do not in company disagree, but are friendly; but that there is a core in their hearts, he doubts, which is not to be easily removed; for these men do suffer only for their constancy to the [Chancellor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/804/), or at least from the King’s ill-will against him: that they do now all they can to vilify the clergy, and do accuse [Rochester](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10263/) [Dolben] … [of his being given to boys and of his putting his hand into a gentleman (who now comes to bear evidence against him) his codpiece while they were at table together. – L&M] And so do raise scandals, all that is possible, against other of the Bishops. He do suggest that something is intended for the [Duke of Monmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5315/), and it may be, against [the Queene](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2381/) also: that we are in no manner sure against an invasion the next year: that the [Duke of Buckingham](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2558/) do rule all now, and the Duke of York comes indeed to [the Caball](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13278/), but signifies little there. That this new faction do not endure, nor the King, [Sir W. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/); but yet that he is so usefull that they cannot be without him; but that he is not now called to the Caball. That my Lord of Buckingham, [Bristoll](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2845/), and [Arlington](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5520/), do seem to agree in these things; but that they do not in their hearts trust one another, but do drive several ways, all of them. In short, he do bless himself that he is no more concerned in matters now; and the hopes he hath of being at liberty, when his accounts are over, to retire into the country. That he do give over the kingdom for wholly lost. So after some other little discourse, I away, meeting with [Mr. Cooling](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1027/). I with him by coach to [the Wardrobe](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/946/), where I never was since [the fire](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10319/) in [Hatton Garden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10948/), but did not ’light: and he tells me he fears that my [Lord Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) will suffer much by [Mr. Townsend’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/947/) being untrue to him, he being now unable to give the [Commissioners of the Treasury](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11226/) an account of his money received by many thousands of pounds, which I am troubled for.

Thence to the [Old Exchange](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/) together, he telling me that he believes there will be no such turning out of great men as is talked of, but that it is only to fright people, but I do fear there may be such a thing doing. He do mightily inveigh against the folly of the King to bring his matters to wrack thus, and that we must all be undone without help. I met with Cooling at the [Temple-gate](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/503/), after I had been at both [my](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11024/)[booksellers](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11465/) and there laid out several pounds in books now against the new year. From the ’Change (where I met with [Captain Cocke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), who would have borrowed money of me, but I had the grace to deny him, he would have had 3 or 400 _l._) I with Cocke and [Mr. Temple](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9022/) (whose wife was just now brought to bed of a boy, but he seems not to be at all taken with it, which is a strange consideration how others do rejoice to have a child born), to Sir G. Carteret’s, in [Lincoln’s Inn Fields](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/125/), and there did dine together, there being there, among other company, [Mr. Attorney Montagu](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/563/), and [his fine lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3690/), a fine woman. After dinner, I did understand from my [Lady Jemimah](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/114/) that her brother [Hinchingbroke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/113/) business was to be ended this day, as she thinks, towards his match, and they do talk here of their intent to buy themselves some new clothes against the wedding, which I am very glad of. After dinner I did even with Sir G. Carteret the accounts of the interest of the money which I did so long put out for him in [Sir R. Viner’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8584/) hands, and by it I think I shall be a gainer about 28 _l._, which is a very good reward for the little trouble I have had in it. Thence with [Sir Philip Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8250/) to the [King’s playhouse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/475/), there to see [“Love’s Cruelty,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11973/) an old play, but which I have not seen before; and in the first act [Orange Moll](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10310/) come to me, with one of our porters by my house, to tell me that [Mrs. Pierce](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/785/) and [Knepp](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9483/) did dine at my house to-day, and that I was desired to come [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/). So I went out presently, and by coach home, and they were just gone away so, after a very little stay with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), I took coach again, and to the King’s playhouse again, and come in the fourth act; and it proves to me a very silly play, and to everybody else, as far as I could judge. But the jest is, that here telling Moll how I had lost my journey, she told me that Mrs. Knepp was in the house, and so shews me to her, and I went to her, and sat out the play, and then with her to [Mrs. Manuel’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11497/), where Mrs. Pierce was, and her [boy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9472/) and [girl](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9044/); and here I did hear Mrs. Manuel and one of the Italians, her gallant, sing well. But yet I confess I am not delighted so much with it, as to admire it: for, not understanding the words, I lose the benefit of the vocalitys of the musick, and it proves only instrumental; and therefore was more pleased to hear Knepp sing two or three little English things that I understood, though the composition of the other, and performance, was very fine. Thence, after sitting and talking a pretty while, I took leave and left them there, and so to my bookseller’s, and paid for the books I had bought, and away home, where I told my wife where I had been. But she was as mad as a devil, and nothing but ill words between us all the evening while we sat at [cards](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/797/) — [W. Hewer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1082/) and [the girl](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11640/) by — even to gross ill words, which I was troubled for, but do see that I must use policy to keep her spirit down, and to give her no offence by my being with Knepp and Pierce, of which, though she will not own it, yet she is heartily jealous. At last it ended in few words and my silence (which for fear of growing higher between us I did forbear), and so to supper and to bed without one word one to another.

This day I did carry money out, and paid several debts. Among others, [my tailor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9587/), and shoemaker, and draper, [Sir W. Turner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3725/), who begun to talk of the [Commission of accounts](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/12029/), wherein he is one; but though they are the greatest people that ever were in the nation as to power, and like to be our judges, yet I did never speak one word to him of desiring favour, or bidding him joy in it, but did answer him to what he said, and do resolve to stand or fall by my silent preparing to answer whatever can be laid to me, and that will be my best proceeding, I think. This day I got a little rent in my new fine [camlett](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11928/) cloak with the latch of Sir G. Carteret’s door; but it is darned up at my tailor’s, that it will be no great blemish to it; but it troubled me. I could not but observe that Sir Philip Carteret would fain have given me my going into a play; but yet, when he come to the door, he had no money to pay for himself, I having refused to accept of it for myself, but was fain; and I perceive he is known there, and do run upon the score for plays, which is a shame; but I perceive always he is in want of money.[1](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/#fn1-1667-12-30)

In the pit I met with [Sir Ch. North](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/725/), formerly Mr. North, who was with my Lord at sea; and he, of his own accord, was so silly as to tell me he [is married](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11974/); and for her quality (being a Lord’s daughter, my Lord Grey), and person, and beauty, and years, and estate, and disposition, he is the happiest man in the world. I am sure he is an ugly fellow; but a good scholar and sober gentleman; and heir to his father, now [Lord North](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/726/), the [old Lord](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/14142/) being dead.

1.   The practice of gallants attending the theatre without payment is illustrated by Mr. Lowe in his “Betterton,” from Shadwell’s “True Widow”:

>

> 
> 
> 4th Man. No; I don’t intend to stay.

>

# [Tuesday 31 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/31/)

Up, without words to [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), or few, and those not angry, and so to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there waited a long time, while the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) was with [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) in [the Caball](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13278/), and there I and [Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/) stayed talking without, in the [Vane-Room](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7036/), and I perceive all people’s expectation is, what will be the issue of this great business of putting these great Lords out of the council and power, the quarrel, I perceive, being only their standing against the will of the King in the business of [the Chancellor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/804/). Anon the Duke of York comes out, and then to a [committee of Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5243/), where my [Lord Middleton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7228/) did come to-day, and seems to me but a dull, heavy man; but he is a great soldier, and stout, and a needy Lord, which will still keep that poor garrison from ever coming to be worth anything to the King. Here, after a short meeting, we broke up, and I home to the office, where they are sitting, and so I to them, and having done our business rose, and I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner with my people, and there dined with me my uncle [Thomas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2542/), with a mourning hat-band on, for his daughter [Mary](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2934/), and here I and my people did discourse of the [Act for the accounts](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/12029/), which do give the greatest power to these people, as they report that have read it (I having not yet read it, and indeed its nature is such as I have no mind to go about to read it, for fear of meeting matter in it to trouble me), that ever was given to any subjects, and too much also. After dinner with my wife and [girl](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11640/) to [Unthanke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1201/), and there left her, and I to Westminster, and there to [Mrs. Martin’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1157/), and did hazer con elle what I desired, and there did drink with her, and find fault with [her husband’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7729/) wearing of too fine clothes, by which I perceive he will be a beggar, and so after a little talking I away and took up my wife again, and so home and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where [Captain Perryman](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10970/) did give me an account, walking in the garden, how the seamen of England are discouraged by want of money (or otherwise by being, as he says, but I think without cause, by their being underrated) so far as that he thinks the greatest part are gone abroad or going, and says that it is known that there are Irish in the town, up and down, that do labour to entice the seamen out of the nation by giving them 3 _l._ in hand, and promise of 40 _s._ per month, to go into the [King of France’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5855/) service, which is a mighty shame, but yet I believe is true. I did advise with him about my little vessel, [“The Maybolt,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11665/) which he says will be best for me to sell, though my employing her to [Newcastle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7005/) this winter, and the next spring, for coles, will be a gainful trade, but yet make me great trouble, but I will think of it, and so to my office, ended my letters, and so home to supper and to bed, good friends with my wife.

Thus ends the year, with great happiness to myself and family as to health and good condition in the world, blessed be God for it! only with great trouble to my mind in reference to the publick, there being little hopes left but that the whole nation must in a very little time be lost, either by troubles at home, the [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/) being dissatisfied, and the King led into unsettled councils by some about him, himself considering little, and divisions growing between the King and Duke of York; or else by foreign invasion, to which we must submit if any, at this bad point of time, should come upon us, which the King of France is well able to do. These thoughts, and some cares upon me, concerning my standing in this Office when the Committee of Parliament shall come to examine our Navy matters, which they will now shortly do. I pray God they may do the kingdom service therein, as they will have sufficient opportunity of doing it!

# Summary

Sir Edward Mountagu (Earl of Sandwich): Summary
**By [jeannine](https://www.pepysdiary.com/account/profile/83/), October 2007.**

## Biographies and Portraits

Edward Mountagu (also referred to as _Montagu_), the Earl of Sandwich as depicted by [artist Peter Lely here](http://www.nmm.ac.uk/server/show/conMediaFile.2836) and from the [National Portrait Gallery](http://www.npg.org.uk/live/search/person.asp?search=ss&sText=edward+montagu&LinkID=mp03968), was the generous benefactor and patron of Samuel Pepys. Several wonderful websites offer excellent short biographies and related background information on Lord Sandwich: [British Civil Wars](http://www.british-civil-wars.co.uk/biog/montagu.htm); [1911 Encyclopedia](http://www.1911encyclopedia.org/Edward_Montagu_Sandwich); [Mountagu’s Regiment site](http://montagus.org.uk/edward%20montagu%20himself.htm); [Montague Millennium](http://www.montaguemillennium.com/familyresearch/h_1672_edward.htm); [Hinchingbrooke House](http://www.hinchhouse.org.uk/edward/edward2.html). For those subscribing to the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, the biography by J.D. Davies is well worth reading.

Sandwich’s surviving papers and letters are located in the British Museum and the Bodleian Library at Oxford. In the Clive Powell article referenced below, it appears that the Montagu family sold the remaining family papers to the National Maritime Museum. Powell tells us that the 5 volumes acquired from the family cover the period of 1656-1669 (overlapping Sam’s Diary) and provide “many insights into a soldier, politician, diplomat and naval commander who moved from one side to the other of the political divide”. In addition, there are letters between Pepys and Sandwich in the Maritime collection.

## “My Lord” in the Diary

Prior to the Diary Mountagu was a strong supporter of Oliver Cromwell and upon his death, supported his son Richard for the role of Protector. With the overthrow of Richard in April 1659, Mountagu slipped out of the political whirlwind, moved back to Hinchingbrooke, and remained publicly silent as the political factions maneuvered for control. In the first few months of the Diary, Mountagu secretly transitioned his loyalties to the Royalist cause and supported the reinstatement of [Charles II](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/). He was elected as a member of the [Council of State](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/02/23/), [co-General at Sea](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/03/03/) (a role he shared with [Monck](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/)), and Commissioner of the Admiralty. He prepared the fleet for the Restoration of the King and set sail (with Pepys on board), welcomed Charles II on board the [Naseby](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/462/) on [May 23, 1660](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/05/23/) and arrived in Dover [two days later](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1660/05/25/). In return for this dutiful service Charles II made Mountagu the first Earl of Sandwich, Knight of the Garter and Master of the Wardrobe.

Sandwich was given honorable naval duties including bringing other Royal exiles home to England, arranging for the cession of Tangier and bringing the betrothed Queen, [Catherine of Braganza](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2381/) (and a portion of her promised dowry) from her homeland of Portugal. These activities, captured so well by Pepys in his Diary were also recorded first hand by Sandwich in his own [Journal](http://www.pepysdiary.com/indepth/2006/05/02/the-journal-of-my-/).

In 1663, Sandwich, who had been ill early in the year, spent visibly less time at the King’s Court. During much of this time away he was taking care of family matters, although gossip began regarding an alleged relationship with a girl in Chelsea. As the gossip became more rampant, Sam decided to send his Lord a [letter of reproof](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/11/18/), which brought an abrupt stop to Sandwich’s visits to Chelsea, but perhaps damaged the closeness between the two men.

In early 1665 during the [Second Dutch War](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Dutch_War) Sandwich had great success as a naval commander in the first [Battle of Lowestoft](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lowestoft) . Later that year his reputation was unfortunately marred by the “prize-goods” incident and Sandwich was subsequently relived of his command. In 1666 he was sent to Spain as an Ambassador, where he remained until 1668. During this time he proved his value through his tactful negotiation and mediation, which led to an end to the ongoing war between Spain and Portugal.

After Sam’s Diary ended, Sandwich returned to Naval duty and took an active role commanding a squadron in the Third Dutch War. He died aboard the [Royal James](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3124/) during the [Battle of Solebay](http://www.tosd.demon.co.uk/battle.htm) in May of 1672. He was given a well-deserved hero’s funeral, regaining in his death the grand status that his lifetime of achievements so well deserved.

## His Character

Sandwich’s biographers and contemporaries offer interesting insights into Sandwich’s character. In his ODNB article, J. D. Davies states that:

> If Sandwich was often the subject of popular and political attack in life, his reputation was fortunate in death. The publication of Pepys’s diary presented a picture of his “my lord” almost as a true Renaissance man: the generous patron, the cheerful if sometimes moody companion, the hopeless manager of money, the competent artist and musician. He had an ear for languages, mastering Spanish by the end of his embassy, and his fascination with topography, mathematics, astronomy, and navigation emerges clearly from his manuscript journals.

The F.R. Harris biography offers a detailed character sketch of Sandwich, from which the following condensed sections are quoted:

> The interest in Lord Sandwich’s life lies in achievement rather than in character, but some fragments of evidence may be collected to show what manner of man he was… He was excellent company, even for the King; though he made no epigrams like Buckingham or Rochester, he could deliver himself of an occasional droll remark, which balanced the want of a ready and scintillating wit. He was tolerant in opinion… For political intrigue he had no relish. His lonely youth gave him a certain detachment of opinion, and an independence of judgment, which made him appear a trimmer. In reality he lacked finesse; he put his country first, and followed whom he liked; he put principles before persons. He hated disorder, and he hated persecution. Three times he chose his path, and each time for security and good government. He left Manchester, who was weak, for Cromwell, who was strong; he left Cromwell when the law was outraged; he left Richard when he felt that Richard was incapable. His passion for order made him a monarchist; it mattered little whether Cromwell or Charles Stewart were King. And since he saw the Stewart monarchy was bound up with settled law and an established Church, he favored uniformity. Dissent spelt difference, and to Sandwich a settled horizon was all that mattered. He had been in England throughout all her troubles, and detested those who bade fair to shake the settlement.
> 
> 
> To his friends he was kindly and affectionate, not one of those who, in fickle times, rejoiced over the misfortunes of others. He bore no malice, and forgave as he had been forgiven… His friends were young and well-informed, and were not chosen for their political influence. Sandwich was as happy with John Evelyn, Sam Pepys… as he was with the most influential statesman… Any estrangement that came between Sandwich and Pepys was not due only to my Lord… The politician whom Sandwich best knew was Lord Clarendon, and everywhere in Clarendon’s writings Sandwich is spoken of with the greatest warmth, and not as one who ever acted the part of an enemy.
> 
> 
> It is a pity that he was careless over money matters, but it was a carelessness which quickly brought its own punishment, and for which he suffered and paid… The mistake over the prize-goods came of this flaw in Sandwich’s character, and can be excused upon no other grounds… Kind as a father, affectionate as a husband, it would scarcely be necessary to touch upon My Lords’ moral character were it not that he is the victim of an unfortunate mistake. The indictment brought against him [see Wheatley’s, _Samuel Pepys And the World He Lived In_, page 175], that he was of ‘a committee with somebody else for getting of Mrs. Stewart for the King’ does not refer to Lord Sandwich [but to his cousin Edward Mountagu], and the indictment breaks down ([see the November 6, 1663 entry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1663/11/06/)). Pepys, in addition to the Becke incident, gives some gossip about Lady Castlemaine, but in no case has he anything to offer worthy of credence. …Evelyn speaks of Sandwich as sober and chaste, while the Puritans regarded him as one who could check the spirit of profaneness then upon the nation.
> 
> 
> The mists of enmity cannot obscure his ability as a naval commander. He began his career at the age of thirty, without any previous training; he was conjoined in the command with one of our greatest Admirals, and proved a ready and an apt pupil, worthy of a higher place than that allotted to him in the ranks of our great seaman. His sailors appreciated, loved, and revered him. His powers of discipline were at once shown to be effective; through he never treated the men with undue harshness. In later years, he was looked upon as rather too lenient to them, but that was when cruelty was rife. From the age of eighteen he had been accustomed to leadership; he had the necessary sympathy and power, and his jovial personality gave him the right temper for the work.
> 
> 
> To state his exact contribution is impossible, but the man who outmaneuvered the Dutch in the Sound, who anticipated the Vicomte de Morogues’ idea of tactical concentration, who led through the enemy’s line off Lowestoft, who drew up the instructions for 1665, and who endeavored to save our fleet from the errors perpetrated in the third Dutch war, must be allowed at least a flash of the genius which inspired the greatest of his successors. In the end he showed that he was of the stuff of which seamen are made. His career was fitly crowned by the bravery of his last fight: the way in which he bore the brunt of the battle, and the manner of his death, are eloquent of his tenacity and courage. He wiped out all stains, and the pageantry of his funeral was a worthy memorial. In a conclave of seamen he need no longer sit below the salt.

Both Ollard and Davies leave the final words about Lord Sandwich to his contemporary and friend, the dignified and highly perceptive John Evelyn who recorded in his diary on May 31, 1672:

> My L: Sandwich was prudent as well as Valiant, & allways govern’d his affairs with successe, and little losse, he was for deliberation & reason… Thus this gallant Person perish’d … & deplorable was the losse, of one of the best accomplish[ed] persons, not onely of this Nation but of any other: He was learned in Mathematics, in Musique, in Sea affaires, in Political: Had ben divers Embassies, was of a sweet obliging temper, Sober, Chast, infinitly ingenious & a true noble man, an ornament to the Court & his Prince, nor has he left any that approach his many Virtues behind him … I am yet heartily griev’d at this mightly losse, nor do I call it to my thoughts without emotion.

## Further Resources

Biographies about Lord Sandwich and his Journal are listed below. These books tend to be rare and may be available through your local library (with the help of the research department) or are sometimes available through the [used book search](http://www.usedbooksearch.co.uk/books.htm).

*   _The Life of Edward Mountagu, K.G. First Earl of Sandwich, (1625-1672)_ by Frank Reginald Harris
*   _Cromwell’s Earl: A Life of Edward Mountagu, 1st Earl of Sandwich_ by Richard Ollard
*   _The Journal of Edward Montagu: First Earl of Sandwich, Admiral and General at Sea_, 1659-1665 (Publications of the Navy Records Society)
*   _Oxford Dictionary of National Biography_ article entitled ‘Montagu, Edward’ by J. D. Davies, (note: this is an online paid subscription service)
*   ‘The papers of Edward Montagu, first Earl of Sandwich (1625-72)’ by Clive Powell of the National Maritime Museum appearing in the _Mariner’s Mirror_ volume 84 issue 4 (November 1998): 470 ff.

**Edward Montagu, 1st Earl of Sandwich** (27 July 1625 – 28 May 1672), was an English military officer, politician and diplomat from [Barnwell, Northamptonshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnwell,_Northamptonshire "Barnwell, Northamptonshire"). During the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War") he served with the [Parliamentarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead") army, and was a member of the [Parliament of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England") at various times between 1645 and 1660. Under [the Protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Protectorate "The Protectorate"), he was also a member of the [English Council of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Council_of_State "English Council of State") and [General at sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_at_sea "General at sea").

In the political infighting that followed the death of [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") in 1658, he played an important role in bringing about the [Stuart Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Restoration "Stuart Restoration") in May 1660. Created [Earl of Sandwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Sandwich "Earl of Sandwich") by [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England"), he served as [Ambassador to Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_Kingdom_of_England_to_Portugal "List of ambassadors of the Kingdom of England to Portugal") from 1661 to 1662. He was appointed [Ambassador to Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_Kingdom_to_Spain "List of ambassadors of the United Kingdom to Spain") in 1666 and helped to negotiate the [1667 Treaty of Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Madrid_(1667) "Treaty of Madrid (1667)").

When the [Second Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Dutch_War "Second Anglo-Dutch War") began in 1665, he commanded a naval [squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squadron_(naval) "Squadron (naval)") but was later suspended in a dispute over [prize money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prize_(law) "Prize (law)"). He was restored to command when the [Third Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Anglo-Dutch_War "Third Anglo-Dutch War") began in May 1672, but was killed at the [Battle of Solebay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Solebay "Battle of Solebay") in June. Montagu is one of the best-known characters of the 1660s, being a central figure in the diaries of his distant cousin the naval official [Samuel Pepys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys "Samuel Pepys").

## Personal details

Edward Montagu was born on 25 July 1625 as the only surviving son of [Sir Sidney Montagu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Montagu_(MP,_died_1644) "Sidney Montagu (MP, died 1644)") (c. 1572–1644) and his first wife, Paulina Pepys (died 1638), great-aunt of [Samuel Pepys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys "Samuel Pepys"). On 7 November 1642 Edward married Jemimah Crew, daughter of [John Crew, 1st Baron Crew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Crew,_1st_Baron_Crew "John Crew, 1st Baron Crew"), and Jemima Waldegrave, whom Pepys in his diary refers to with great affection as "My Lady". The couple had ten children:[[1]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTELatham2000255-1)

*   Jemima (1646–1671)
*   [Edward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_2nd_Earl_of_Sandwich "Edward Montagu, 2nd Earl of Sandwich") (1648–1688)
*   Paulina (1649–1669)
*   [Sidney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Wortley_Montagu "Sidney Wortley Montagu") (1650–1727)
*   [Oliver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Montagu "Oliver Montagu") (c. 1655–1689)
*   [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Montagu_(Trinity) "John Montagu (Trinity)") (c. 1655–1729)
*   [Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Montagu_(died_1721) "Charles Montagu (died 1721)") (1658–1721)
*   Anne (1660–1729)
*   Catherine (1661–1757)
*   James (b. 1664)

Paulina's death in February 1669, aged only twenty, was a great source of grief to her father. Pepys, who called her "a peevish lady", called to pay his condolences, but found him "shut away for sorrow".[[2]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOllard1994248-2)

## First English Civil War and Interregnum

Although his father was a [Royalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier "Cavalier"), when the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War") began in August 1642, Montagu served in the [Eastern Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Association "Eastern Association") army led by his [Parliamentarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead") cousin, [the Earl of Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_2nd_Earl_of_Manchester "Edward Montagu, 2nd Earl of Manchester"). He raised a regiment of infantry which during the 1644 campaign fought at [Marston Moor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marston_Moor "Battle of Marston Moor"), the [Siege of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_York "Siege of York") and [Second Newbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Battle_of_Newbury "Second Battle of Newbury"). Despite his family relationship, Montagu supported those in [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England") who expressed dissatisfaction with the conduct of the war by Manchester and [Essex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Devereux,_3rd_Earl_of_Essex "Robert Devereux, 3rd Earl of Essex").[[3]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTECotton1975212-3)

This resulted in the creation of the [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army") in February 1645 and the passing of the [Self-denying Ordinance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-denying_Ordinance "Self-denying Ordinance"), requiring those holding military commissions to resign from Parliament. As members of the [House of Lords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Lords "House of Lords"), Manchester and Essex were automatically removed, since unlike MPs they could not resign their titles.[[4]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWedgwood1958398%E2%80%93399-4) Montagu's regiment was incorporated into the New Model, taking part in the June 1645 [Battle of Naseby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Naseby "Battle of Naseby"), followed by the [capture of Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Bristol_(1645) "Siege of Bristol (1645)"). In October he resigned from the army as required by the Ordinance when was appointed MP for [Huntingdonshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huntingdonshire_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Huntingdonshire (UK Parliament constituency)"), a seat formerly held by his father who died in September 1644.[[5]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHealy2010-5)

Montagu played no part in the [Second English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War "Second English Civil War") and retired from Parliament after [Pride's Purge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pride%27s_Purge "Pride's Purge") in December 1648 to live quietly at home. He returned to politics in 1653 when his neighbour [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") nominated him to the [Barebones Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barebones_Parliament "Barebones Parliament") as MP for Huntingdonshire, a seat formerly held by his father who died in September 1644.[[5]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHealy2010-5) He was also appointed to the [English Council of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Council_of_State "English Council of State"), an office he held until it was dissolved in 1659, and was re-elected to the [First Protectorate Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Protectorate_Parliament "First Protectorate Parliament") in 1654, then the [Second Protectorate Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Protectorate_Parliament "Second Protectorate Parliament") in 1656.[[6]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHenning1983-6)

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Edward_Montagu.jpeg/250px-Edward_Montagu.jpeg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edward_Montagu.jpeg)

Portrait of Sandwich by Sir [Peter Lely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Lely "Peter Lely"), painted 1666, part of the [Flagmen of Lowestoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flagmen_of_Lowestoft "Flagmen of Lowestoft") series.

During the [Anglo-Spanish War (1654–1660)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Spanish_War_(1654%E2%80%931660) "Anglo-Spanish War (1654–1660)"), he was appointed joint [General at Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_at_Sea "General at Sea") with [Robert Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Blake_(admiral) "Robert Blake (admiral)"), taking part in an expedition into the [Mediterranean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean "Mediterranean"). This experience made him a leading advocate of establishing a British naval base in the region, an ambition realised with the acquisition of [English Tangier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Tangier "English Tangier") in 1661.[[7]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTECorbett190411-7) In February 1657, he was one of the so-called "New Cromwellians" who supported the [Humble Petition and Advice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humble_Petition_and_Advice "Humble Petition and Advice"), inviting Cromwell to declare himself king and advocating the re-establishment of a national church. The measure was opposed by army radicals including [Charles Fleetwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Fleetwood "Charles Fleetwood") and [John Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lambert_(general) "John Lambert (general)") and ultimately rejected.[[8]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatterall190336%E2%80%9337-8)

In June 1658 he commanded the naval squadron that blockaded [Dunkirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Dunkirk_(1658) "Siege of Dunkirk (1658)") and when Cromwell died in September, Montagu remained loyal to his son and appointed successor [Richard Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell"). During his brief and disastrous rule as [Lord Protector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Protector "Lord Protector"), Montagu remained at sea and in early 1659 was sent to mediate between Sweden and Denmark; however, he was suspected of secret communication with the exiled [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") and the republicans [Algernon Sidney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algernon_Sidney "Algernon Sidney") and [Sir Robert Honywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Honywood_(New_Romney_MP) "Robert Honywood (New Romney MP)") were sent to monitor his activity.[[9]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOllard199462-9) He was recalled and investigated by the newly installed [Rump Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rump_Parliament "Rump Parliament"); although no evidence was found, he was dismissed from command.[[10]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavies2004-10)

## Restoration

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e0/The_arrival_of_King_Charles_II_of_England_in_Rotterdam%2C_may_24_1660_%28Lieve_Pietersz._Verschuier%2C_1665%29.jpg/500px-The_arrival_of_King_Charles_II_of_England_in_Rotterdam%2C_may_24_1660_%28Lieve_Pietersz._Verschuier%2C_1665%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_arrival_of_King_Charles_II_of_England_in_Rotterdam,_may_24_1660_(Lieve_Pietersz._Verschuier,_1665).jpg)

Charles leaves the Dutch Republic for England, 24 May 1660

By the end of 1659 England appeared to be drifting into [anarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarchy "Anarchy"), with widespread demands for new elections and an end to military rule. In February 1660, [George Monck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Monck,_1st_Duke_of_Albemarle "George Monck, 1st Duke of Albemarle"), military commander in Scotland, marched into London and declared his support for the Rump against the Republican faction led by [John Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lambert_(general) "John Lambert (general)"). Montagu resumed command of the navy and was returned as MP for the important port of [Dover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dover_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Dover (UK Parliament constituency)") when elections were held for a [Convention Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_Parliament_(1660) "Convention Parliament (1660)") in April.[[11]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris191243%E2%80%9344-11)

This placed him in a powerful position during negotiations for the [Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Restoration "Stuart Restoration"); when Parliament resolved to proclaim Charles king and invited him to return to England, Montagu commanded the fleet that brought him from the [Dutch Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Republic "Dutch Republic") on 24 May.[[12]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHutton1989131-12) Two months later, on 12 July 1660, he was created **Baron Montagu of St Neots**, **Viscount Hinchingbrooke**, and **Earl of Sandwich**. King Charles also made him a [Knight of the Garter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Garter "Order of the Garter") and appointed him [Master of the Great Wardrobe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_the_Great_Wardrobe "Master of the Great Wardrobe"), [Admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admiral "Admiral") of the narrow seas (the [English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Channel "English Channel") and southern [North Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sea "North Sea")), and [Lieutenant Admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_Admiral "Lieutenant Admiral") to [The Duke of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_II_of_England "James II of England"), [Lord High Admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Admiralty "British Admiralty") of England. He carried [St. Edward's staff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sceptre_with_the_Cross "Sceptre with the Cross") at Charles' subsequent coronation. [Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon "Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon"), who liked and admired Sandwich, wrote that the conferring of these honours caused much resentment among those Royalists who had gone into exile with their King, and regarded Sandwich as a "diehard" Cromwellian; yet adds that his charm of manner made it almost impossible to dislike him.

He was appointed [Ambassador to Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_Kingdom_of_England_to_Portugal "List of ambassadors of the Kingdom of England to Portugal") in 1661, and strongly favoured the Portuguese marriage, through which England obtained [Mumbai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombay "Bombay") and [Tangier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Tangier "English Tangier"). Sandwich, like others, saw a great future for Tangier as an international trade centre, and he commanded the fleet which took possession of the city in January 1662, purchasing a house there. Returning to England, in his capacity as Ambassador, he escorted the new Queen, [Catherine of Braganza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_of_Braganza "Catherine of Braganza"), from [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon").[[13]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOllard1994109-13)

Montagu was a signatory to _The Several Declarations of The Company of Royal Adventurers of England Trading into Africa_, a document published in 1667 which led to the expansion of the [Royal Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_African_Company "Royal African Company").[[14]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-auto-16)

## The Prize Goods Scandal

In the [Second Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Dutch_War "Second Anglo-Dutch War") of 1665 to 1667 he fought at the [Battle of Lowestoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lowestoft "Battle of Lowestoft"), an English victory, but defeat at the [Battle of Vågen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_V%C3%A5gen "Battle of Vågen") led to him being removed from active service. His reputation suffered another serious blow when he failed to prevent his sailors from plundering a number of Dutch [VOC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_East_India_Company "Dutch East India Company")[prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prize_(law) "Prize (law)") ships, loaded with precious spices from the [East Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Indies "East Indies"), which he had brought in. By long-standing custom the sailors could take any goods they found between the decks, but they were strictly forbidden to "break the bulk" i.e. ransack the ship's hold; yet this is just what Sandwich, an easy-going man with a notoriously poor understanding of money matters, permitted. When this became widely known, the rumour spread that Sandwich had unlawfully helped himself to a fortune (in fact he seems to have taken less than he was entitled to), and the public, who were still enduring the horrors of the [Great Plague of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Plague_of_London "Great Plague of London"), reacted with such unexpected fury that a minor mishap became a national affair: "the Prize Goods Scandal". Although Clarendon wrote that Sandwich was too likeable to have any personal enemies, he did have political opponents, including his own superior at the Admiralty, [James, Duke of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_II_of_England "James II of England"), and James' influential secretary [Sir William Coventry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Coventry "William Coventry"), who were happy to exploit the scandal. He felt obliged to obtain a [royal pardon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_pardon "Royal pardon"): the King, mindful of his good services at the Restoration, willingly granted it.[[17]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOllard1994140%E2%80%93142-17)[[16]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-auto-16)

## Ambassador to Spain

During his absence from battle, Sandwich served as England's ambassador to Spain, replacing [Sir Richard Fanshawe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Richard_Fanshawe,_1st_Baronet "Sir Richard Fanshawe, 1st Baronet"). This is further evidence that despite his unpopularity, he retained the King's confidence, although his political fortunes, like those of his friend and patron Clarendon, were in decline. Sandwich himself had told Pepys the previous year not to put too much reliance on the friendship of any "great man". After the [Great Fire of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London "Great Fire of London") Sandwich downplayed the damage to the Spanish King, claiming that London's slums were the only thing in ashes. This slant on the events was also practised by England's ambassadors throughout Europe.[[18]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-18)

As Ambassador his most notable achievement was the [Anglo-Spanish Commercial Treaty of 1667](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Madrid_(1667) "Treaty of Madrid (1667)"), which laid the foundations for a prosperous trading relationship between the two countries which lasted for over a century.[[19]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-19) He also acted as mediator in the peace negotiations between Spain and Portugal which resulted in the [Treaty of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Lisbon_(1668) "Treaty of Lisbon (1668)"). Like all Ambassadors of the era, he found the cost of running an embassy ruinous (he had never had a good head for business) and on his return to England in the autumn of 1668 one of his first actions was to borrow money from his cousin Samuel Pepys.[[20]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-20) On his way back from Spain, he again visited Tangier to report on the condition of the garrison there.

In 1670 he escorted the King's sister [Henrietta of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrietta_of_England "Henrietta of England"), [Duchess of Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchess_of_Orleans "Duchess of Orleans"), from France to England to negotiate the [Secret Treaty of Dover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secret_Treaty_of_Dover "Secret Treaty of Dover") between her brother and [Louis XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIV "Louis XIV"). Of the existence of the Treaty's secret clauses, notably that by which Charles II pledged to convert to the [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic "Roman Catholic") faith, Sandwich, like the general public, was quite unaware.[[21]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOllard1994253%E2%80%934-21) In the same year he was appointed President of the Privy Council Committee on Foreign Plantations; he had always had a keen interest in international trade, despite his notorious inability to keep his own finances in order.

## Last campaign and death

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Edward_Montagu%2C_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich_by_Sir_Peter_Lely.jpg/250px-Edward_Montagu%2C_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich_by_Sir_Peter_Lely.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich_by_Sir_Peter_Lely.jpg)

Montagu in the 1660s

He was subsequently reappointed to a naval command, and by 1672 at the start of the [Third Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Anglo-Dutch_War "Third Anglo-Dutch War"), he was Vice-Admiral of the Blue with the [_Royal James_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Royal_James "HMS Royal James") as his flagship. At the [Battle of Solebay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Solebay "Battle of Solebay") on 28 May, his ship was attacked by a group of [fire ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_ships "Fire ships") and was destroyed with the loss of many lives, including Sandwich himself. His body was washed ashore a week later, recognisable only from his clothing; it was unmarked and he appeared to have drowned.[[10]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavies2004-10) Sandwich opposed the war and is said to have predicted his own death. Certainly, he told his friend [John Evelyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Evelyn "John Evelyn"), just before he sailed, that "he would see him no more".[[22]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOllard1994256-22)

On Wednesday 3 July 1672 he was buried in [Westminster Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey") after a [state funeral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_funeral "State funeral") that started with a procession along the [River Thames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames "River Thames") of five decorated barges from [Deptford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deptford "Deptford"). His body was landed at [Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster "Westminster") at about 5 pm and carried to the Abbey in a grand procession.[[23]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOllard1994262%E2%80%933-23)

## Sandwich and Samuel Pepys

Sandwich on his mother's side was the first cousin of John Pepys, the father of [Samuel Pepys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys "Samuel Pepys"). Pepys started his career as a minor member of the Sandwich household and owed his appointments first to the Wardrobe and then as Clerk of the Acts to the [Navy Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navy_Board "Navy Board") to Sandwich's influence. Pepys' diary provides a detailed [primary source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_source "Primary source") of Sandwich's career in the 1660s.

They had a serious quarrel in 1663, when Pepys reprimanded Sandwich for living openly with his mistress, Elizabeth Becke, at her "mean house" in [Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea,_London "Chelsea, London").[[24]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOllard1994116%E2%80%937-24) Pepys was concerned at the damage to their family's reputation, Sandwich's neglect of his official duties (thus risking the loss of any remaining influence he had at Court) and also at the insult to Sandwich's wife, to whom Pepys was deeply attached. Following a brief estrangement, friendly relations were resumed, although the two men were probably never as close again as they had been (Pepys, for example, is not mentioned in Sandwich's last will). For Pepys to raise the issue at all took considerable courage, considering how much he owed to his patron, and his Diary shows that he was strongly tempted to let the matter lie. Even when he did raise it he chose to write rather than confront Sandwich face to face.

In 1668 Pepys was somewhat perturbed when his wife [Elizabeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elisabeth_Pepys "Elisabeth Pepys"), during one of the violent quarrels which followed the discovery of his affair with her companion [Deb Willet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deb_Willet "Deb Willet"), told him that Sandwich had asked her to be his mistress.[[25]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-25) Since Pepys was in no doubt that she had refused, he decided to treat the matter as being closed, and friendly relations continued: Sandwich dined at their house for the first time a few months later.[[26]](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#cite_note-26) Pepys, on reflection, may have thought it possible that Elizabeth in her anger had invented the story to upset him, (as she undoubtedly invented the story that she was attending [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic "Roman Catholic") services). Whatever their differences, Pepys in later life always remembered Sandwich, whom he called "that noble and unparalleled Lord", and his wife (who died in 1674) with affection and gratitude.

### David Gurliacci on 1 Jan 2003•[Link](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/#c41 "Link directly to this annotation")

Montagu as of Jan. 1, 1660:

One of Cromwell's young colonels in the Civil War, Montagu broke with extremists in the army in 1648 but became a member of Parliament in 1653. Later that year he was made a "councillor of state" in the government.

Montagu had supported every proposal to make the protectorate hereditary and even the radical proposal to make Cromwell king. He also supported Cromwell's son, Richard, when he became protector.

When Richard fell from power in 1659, Montagu "distanced himself, in common with many other moderates, from the revolutionary cause," Robert Latham writes in his introduction to "The Shorter Pepys," a 1990 abridgement of the diary.

In the spring or summer of 1659 Montagu communicated with agents of Charles II. Montagu was suspected of disloyalty to the government and by winter he had retired to his country estate, Hinchingbrooke. Pepys remained in charge of his affairs in London.
